The Ecosystem

DifferentialGames.jl is a family of five packages. This page explains what each one is for, how they depend on each other, and how a problem flows from a model to a result, a learned policy or a benchmark score.

The packages

PackageRoleDepends onProvides
DifferentialGamesBase.jlLanguage of the ecosystem: problem types, dynamics, costs, constraints, solutions, and the solver contract— (ForwardDiff, LinearAlgebra, SparseArrays)GameProblem and the other problem types, PlayerSpec, GNEPSolution, GameSolver, solve, solver_capabilities, uncertainty propagation and chance constraints
DifferentialGamesBaseSolvers.jlModel-based solversBaseFNELQ, SFNELQ, iLQGames, ALGAMES, LIBR, YiPavel, InverseLQGames, RecedingHorizonNash, DynamicTubeMPC, DGSQP; a Plots extension and an extension for the soft dependency FALCON
DifferentialGames.jl (this package)Umbrella and documentation: one using for Base + SolversBase, SolversReexports both; this manual
DifferentialGamesMARL.jlLearning-based solvers: multi-agent reinforcement learningBase, Solvers (+ Flux, Optimisers, CommonRLInterface)MADDPGEnv, MADDPGSolver, guided policy search, benchmark tasks
DifferentialGamesBenchmarks.jlEvaluation: benchmark cases, challenge transformations, independent metricsBase (Solvers and Makie as extensions)BenchmarkCases, Experiment, evaluators and plots

None of the five packages is in the General registry yet, so they are installed by URL (see Installation). using DifferentialGames loads only Base and Solvers; MARL and Benchmarks are separate installs because they bring heavy dependencies (Flux, Makie).

Dependency structure

Arrows read "depends on".

PackageDepends on
DifferentialGamesDifferentialGamesBase, DifferentialGamesBaseSolvers
DifferentialGamesBaseSolversDifferentialGamesBase
DifferentialGamesMARLDifferentialGamesBase, DifferentialGamesBaseSolvers (used for the local FNELQ step)
DifferentialGamesBenchmarksDifferentialGamesBase; DifferentialGamesBaseSolvers and Makie only as extensions

Everything depends on Base. A new solver package needs only Base; see Writing a solver.

One game, several routes

All routes start from a game object built from Base types. What differs is what consumes it.

RouteEntry pointReturnsPackage
Model-basedsolve(game, solver) with FNELQ, iLQGames, ALGAMES, …GNEPSolutionSolvers
Learning-basedtrain!(MADDPGSolver(…), MADDPGEnv(game))trained agents and learning historiesMARL
Learning guided by a modelthe same, with gps_builder(DeterministicLQNash())trained agentsMARL, calling FNELQ from Solvers
Evaluationevaluate(evaluator, game(case), sol) for any solutionvalidity, quality, robustness and efficiency metricsBenchmarks

Two contracts hold the ecosystem together:

  1. The solver contract (Base). A solver is a subtype of GameSolver with solver_capabilities and a _solve(game, solver, warmstart, verbose) method. Anything that follows it works with solve, with RecedingHorizonNash and with the Benchmarks Experiment.
  2. The solution contract (Base). Model-based solvers return a GNEPSolution (or a problem-specific solution type) with trajectories, strategies, converged and solver_info. Evaluators and plots read this object only.

The learning route does not go through solve: MADDPGSolver is a plain configuration struct and is run with train!(solver, env), which returns agents and learning histories rather than a GNEPSolution. A guided policy search step is the point where the two worlds meet: it calls FNELQ from the Solvers package on a local LQ approximation of the same Base game to produce guidance for the learner.

Which package do I need?

I want to…Use
formulate a game and solve it with a model-based methodDifferentialGames (Base + Solvers)
write a new problem type or a new solver in my own packageDifferentialGamesBase only
train neural-network policies on a differential gameDifferentialGamesMARL
compare solvers on standard cases, or test robustness to noise/disturbance/partial observationDifferentialGamesBenchmarks
recover cost parameters from observed playDifferentialGames (InverseLQGames)

A worked route across packages

The example below builds one game in Base, solves it with three different solvers from the Solvers package, and compares the results on the same footing. The learning and benchmarking routes use the identical game object; their code is shown on the MADDPG, environment and Benchmarks pages.

using DifferentialGames, LinearAlgebra

# A linear-quadratic game (Base)
n = 4
game = LQGameProblem(
    Matrix(0.95 * I(n)),
    [Matrix(1.0I(n))[:, 1:1], Matrix(1.0I(n))[:, 3:3]],
    [Matrix(1.0I(n)), Matrix(1.0I(n))],
    [fill(0.1, 1, 1), fill(0.1, 1, 1)],
    [Matrix(10.0I(n)), Matrix(10.0I(n))],
    ones(n), 2.0; dt = 0.1,
)

# Three solvers from the Solvers package, one interface
sols = Dict(name => solve(game, solver) for (name, solver) in
            ("FNELQ" => FNELQ(), "iLQGames" => iLQGames(), "ALGAMES" => ALGAMES()))

for (name, s) in sols
    println(rpad(name, 9), " type = ", rpad(s.equilibrium_type, 14), " converged = ", s.converged,
            "  J = ", round.(get_costs(s); digits = 4))
end
FNELQ     type = FeedbackNash   converged = true  J = [11.268, 11.268]
iLQGames  type = FeedbackNash   converged = true  J = [11.2744, 11.2744]
ALGAMES   type = OpenLoopNash   converged = true  J = [11.268, 11.268]

FNELQ returns the exact feedback Nash costs; iLQGames iterates towards the same value with a regularization-limited rate; ALGAMES returns an open-loop equilibrium, whose cost need not coincide with the feedback one in general. The conventions page lists what is and is not comparable across solvers.
